items.title: [ScienceDaily] Microplastics may be more dangerous than we thought. Scientists just discovered why
items.content_html: Microplastics may be doing something far more dangerous than simply accumulating in our bodies. Scientists have discovered that tiny plastic particles can interact with water to generate highly reactive molecules capable of damaging cells and tissues. This unexpected chemical activity could help explain growing evidence linking microplastic exposure to serious health problems, including heart attacks, strokes, and neurological disorders.

items.title: [scientificamerican.com] Astronomers witness dying giant star engulfing companion in real time
items.content_html: Astronomers watched a dying giant star in the Andromeda galaxy engulf and merge with its smaller companion, recording the process as it unfolded for the first time. The companion spiraled through the giant’s outer envelope for about seven years before the system erupted in October 2025. The observation provides direct evidence of a short-lived phase called common-envelope evolution, previously studied mainly through models. The James Webb Space Telescope observed the remnant 47 days after the eruption, but dust from expelled material now obscures the remnant. Researchers plan to monitor the system as it cools and settles over the coming years or decades.

items.title: [science.org] Brain study finds speech-planning region may aid communication devices
items.content_html: A study published Nov. 19 in Science identifies a small region within Wernicke’s area that helps prepare words before people speak, challenging the view that the area mainly processes speech heard from others. The region, the left posterior superior temporal gyrus, became active before speech, and disrupting it caused speech errors in stimulation and lesion tests. Researchers recorded brain activity in 28 people undergoing treatment for epilepsy or tumors. Stimulation tests involved 13 people, and an analysis of surgical cases also linked damage to the area with speech difficulties. In two people with paralysis, signals from the region helped researchers decode intended and heard speech, suggesting it could be explored as a target for communication devices for people with language disorders. Researchers presented the findings at the Society for Neuroscience meeting on Nov. 15.

items.title: [ScienceDaily] Something strange is living beneath the skin of deep-sea pigs
items.content_html: Scientists have discovered a strange bacterium hiding beneath the skin of deep-sea creatures known as sea pigs, revealing an unexpected biological partnership. The microbe has an unusually tiny genome, yet more than a quarter of its DNA is devoted to making surface proteins, some of them exceptionally large. Researchers suspect it depends heavily on its host for survival, but what the sea pigs gain in return remains a mystery.

items.title: [science.nasa.gov] Webb traces Andromeda star merger, challenging common-envelope models
items.content_html: Astronomers say a smaller star spiraled into a red giant and merged with it in the Andromeda galaxy, marking the first closely tracked observation of this stage of binary-star evolution. The system, named AT 2025abao, brightened over several years before erupting in October 2025. NASA’s James Webb Space Telescope observed it 47 days after the outburst peaked, helping researchers reconstruct the event. The team estimates that the giant had seven times the Sun’s mass and the companion about 0.7 times the Sun’s mass. Their interaction ended after about seven orbits, or seven years. The findings, published in Nature on Nov. 18, indicate that energy transport during the shared-envelope phase may be more complex than standard models describe. Researchers say continued observations are needed to determine the remnant’s state and confirm the merger.

items.title: [ScienceDaily] MIT discovers that aging weakens the brain’s nighttime cleaning system
items.content_html: MIT researchers have discovered that the brain’s natural waste-removal system becomes significantly less effective during sleep as people age. The decline is linked to weaker deep-sleep brain waves and changes in blood flow, potentially offering new clues about why aging increases the risk of Alzheimer's disease and dementia. Surprisingly, some older adults retain the same powerful cleansing waves seen in younger people.

items.title: [gizmodo.com] Pacific nodules targeted by miners harbor thousands of animals
items.content_html: Researchers found 4,139 animals living in or on 244 polymetallic nodules collected from the Pacific’s Clarion-Clipperton Zone, an area targeted for deep-sea mining. The animals sheltered in cracks and cavities in the metal-rich rocks and formed communities distinct from those in the surrounding seafloor sediment. The nodules contain metals including manganese, cobalt and copper. One nodule held as many as 245 animals; the researchers warn that mining could cause irreversible losses among species that have not yet been described. Deep-sea mining remains in technology trials and has not entered full-scale commercial operation.

A new technique developed at UC San Diego could help rule out misleading telescope errors, bringing researchers closer to determining whether the strange signal is real.

items.title: [phys.org] Researchers urge protection of ocean climate refugia as warming intensifies
items.content_html: A review of marine research argues that conservation plans should include ocean climate refugia—areas where conditions help species withstand climate change—as warming, acidification, oxygen loss and other pressures reshape marine ecosystems. Researchers reviewed 798 studies published from 2021 to 2026 and selected 82 that identified or mapped refugia. They found three main approaches: measuring low climate exposure, observing ecological resilience and predicting future habitat suitability. The authors say refugia could guide the designation of marine protected areas and restoration efforts, but substantial research gaps remain in the high seas and deep ocean. Identifying such areas could also help countries plan a network of protected areas under the U.N. High Seas Treaty, which is now in force, they say.

items.title: [Nautilus] There’s New Hope for Detecting Alzheimer’s Before Cognitive Deficits Manifest
items.content_html:
With no cure for Alzheimer’s on the horizon, and our best treatments only slowing the progression of the disease, there’s been an intense effort to find earlier means of detection. Now, a new study published in Neuroimage Reports is offering hope of diagnosis even before cognitive symptoms become noticeable.   

A team of biomedical imaging specialists, pathologists, and neuroscientists from Johns Hopkins University studied how the brains of older adults changed over time by analyzing hundreds of MRI scans and PET scans. They relied on longitudinal data from two different studies (the Alzheimer’s Disease Neuroimaging Initiative and the Biomarkers of Cognitive Decline Among Normal Individuals study) that included people from across the Alzheimer’s spectrum, from cognitively healthy to full-blown dementia.

Read more: “How the Brain’s Failing Trash Compactor Can Contribute to Alzheimer’s Disease”

items.title: [scientificamerican.com] Neanderthal DNA variant linked to smaller visual brain region, lower schizophrenia odds
items.content_html:
🏔️ ✏️

Researchers report that a Neanderthal-derived DNA variant is associated with a smaller occipital lobe and lower odds of schizophrenia in modern humans. In UK Biobank data, each copy of the variant corresponded to about 0.85 cubic centimeters less occipital-lobe volume; people with two copies had nearly 10% lower odds of schizophrenia than those with no copies. The occipital lobe processes visual information. The variant lies near DAAM1, a gene involved in brain development, but researchers have not established how it affects the brain or whether the smaller lobe explains the schizophrenia association. The variant was not associated with a meaningful difference in intelligence, and outside researchers cautioned against drawing conclusions about Neanderthal brain function from the findings in modern humans. The study was published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences. Its authors say further work, including studies using brain organoids or animal models, could investigate the mechanism.

items.title: [sciencealert.com] Florida researchers identify mushroom with psychedelic and deadly toxins
items.content_html: Researchers identified Galerina indica as the first known mushroom to contain both psilocybin, which produces psychedelic effects, and amatoxins, which are linked to fatal mushroom poisonings. The team confirmed the compounds through chemical analysis and genome sequencing after finding specimens in Florida wetlands. The species stains blue when handled, a feature associated with psilocybin that could mislead foragers into assuming it is safe. Researchers said toxin levels in G. indica have not been established. They also found evidence of rare gene transfers in the mushroom’s evolutionary history. Future experiments could disable genes that produce either compound to test their roles in the fungus, the researchers said.

items.title: [sciencealert.com] Studies explore how ancient gases may have formed pure sulfur deposits on Mars
items.content_html: NASA’s Curiosity rover discovered pure elemental sulfur crystals in rocks that broke beneath its wheels in Mars’ Gediz Vallis channel in 2024, the first confirmed discovery of sulfur in that form on the planet. Similar rocks covered about 2,100 square meters, and a study published in June 2026 estimated that the deposit formed between 3.1 billion and 2.8 billion years ago. Researchers propose that sulfur-bearing gases from ancient volcanic activity became trapped underground and later escaped as erosion exposed the deposits. A separate experiment found that dissolved sulfide and chlorate could react in acidic water at room temperature to produce elemental sulfur without high heat or life.

items.title: [ScienceDaily] Hidden ecosystem: Scientists discover 245 animals living inside a single deep-sea rock
items.content_html: Deep beneath the Pacific Ocean, scientists have discovered tiny hidden ecosystems inside metal-rich rocks that take millions of years to form. Researchers examined 244 nodules and found more than 4,100 animals living in their cracks and cavities, including unique communities unlike those in the surrounding seafloor mud. These remarkable miniature habitats could now be threatened by deep-sea mining for valuable metals.
